title: The Myth of Multitasking
subtitle: Why doing two things at once usually means doing both of them less well

paragraphs.text: Few modern boasts are as widely admired as the claim to be a good multitasker. Job advertisements request it, and many of us believe we practise it daily, answering emails during meetings or scrolling through the news while half-watching a film. Yet the term itself is borrowed, rather tellingly, from computing, where it described a machine's ability to run several programs apparently at once. Even there the word concealed a sleight of hand: early computers with a single processor did not run programs simultaneously but alternated between them so rapidly that the user could not tell the difference. Humans, the evidence increasingly suggests, do something similar, but with none of the speed.

The difficulty lies in the architecture of attention. Psychologists have long documented what is known as the psychological refractory period: when people must respond to two stimuli presented in quick succession, their response to the second is delayed, as though it were waiting in a queue for the first to be dealt with. This suggests that, at least for tasks requiring a decision, there is a central bottleneck through which only one operation can pass at a time. Professor David Okafor, who has measured such delays for two decades, likens it to a single-lane bridge that no amount of effort can widen. Highly practised, automatic activities, such as walking or chewing, can proceed alongside others with little interference, which is why we can stroll and talk without stumbling. But when two tasks both demand deliberate thought, one must wait.

What we call multitasking, then, is in most cases rapid task-switching, and switching carries a price. Each time we move from one activity to another, the brain must disengage from the rules of the first and load those of the second, a process that laboratory studies measure in fractions of a second per switch. Such figures sound trivial, yet they accumulate over a working day. Dr Elena Marsh, a cognitive psychologist, argues that the greater cost is not the delay itself but the errors that creep in when the mind returns to a task it has not fully reloaded. Worse, something of the abandoned task appears to linger: in her experiments, participants who were interrupted mid-task performed less well on the next one, even when they had been told to put the first entirely out of their minds.

If switching is costly, one might expect habitual multitaskers to have become adept at it through sheer practice. The evidence points, uncomfortably, the other way. In a much-cited 2009 study, American researchers compared students who reported heavy simultaneous use of several media with those who rarely combined them. The heavy multitaskers were worse, not better, at ignoring irrelevant information, and they were slower when required to switch between tasks. Later studies have been less consistent, some failing to reproduce the effect, which is a reminder that the direction of cause is far from settled. It may be that multitasking erodes the capacity to filter out distraction; it may equally be that people who are already easily distracted are drawn to multitasking. Professor Tomasz Wieczorek favours the second explanation, arguing that the habit is more a symptom than a cause.

There are, admittedly, exceptions. In driving-simulator experiments that required participants to brake for hazards while solving memory problems, a very small minority, around two or three per cent, showed no measurable decline in either task. The publicity that these so-called 'supertaskers' receive is, however, somewhat misleading. Research has found that the people most confident of their ability to multitask are often among those who do it worst, so the existence of a rare elite offers little comfort to the rest of us.

Can the brain, then, be trained to do better? Volunteers who practise a specific pair of tasks for several weeks do improve strikingly, learning to perform both together at far less cost. Dr Ana Ferreira, who has conducted such experiments, is cautiously optimistic, contending that the central bottleneck is not fixed but can be narrowed with sufficient practice. The crucial question, however, is whether these gains transfer to tasks that were not practised. On this point the commercial brain-training industry has been notably less restrained than the scientists. Dr Rajiv Menon, whose team tested a popular training game, found that participants became much better at the game itself but showed no improvement on unrelated measures of attention, a pattern since repeated in many studies. In 2014, around seventy scientists signed an open letter objecting to claims that such products could improve everyday mental performance, and it is hard to disagree with them.

None of this implies that we should never combine activities. Listening to music while running, or folding laundry during a phone call, is harmless precisely because one of the two tasks makes few demands on conscious thought. The problem arises when we pretend that complex, attention-hungry tasks can be carried out in parallel without loss, and when workplaces are designed on that assumption. Nor is the cost borne only by the individual. Studies of hospital wards have linked frequent interruptions to a rise in medication errors, a reminder that in some settings a lapse of attention is measured not in lost minutes but in harm to others. Even in an ordinary office, fragmented attention can masquerade as productivity: a day spent answering every message promptly may feel both exhausting and industrious, yet leave the most demanding work untouched. Constant notifications and the expectation of instant replies oblige employees to switch dozens of times an hour; as the organisational psychologist Dr Laura Brennan puts it, many firms end up rewarding staff for looking busy rather than for what they actually achieve. The more honest response would be to accept the limits of the mind and organise work around them: to protect periods of uninterrupted concentration, and to treat the ability to focus on one thing at a time not as a quaint inefficiency but as the rare and valuable skill it has become.

items.stem: Why does the writer refer to early computers in the first paragraph?
options: to illustrate how rapidly technology has advanced since the early days of computing
to suggest that what looks like doing things simultaneously is really rapid alternation
to argue that machines are more accurate than humans when handling several tasks
to explain why employers have come to value multitasking so highly
items.evidence: did not run programs simultaneously but alternated between them so rapidly that the user could not tell the difference
items.note: A is never suggested - the computers are used as an analogy, not as a measure of progress; C and D are not mentioned in the paragraph.

items.stem: According to the second paragraph, people are able to walk and talk at the same time because
options: walking makes little demand on conscious decision-making.
the two activities are controlled by separate areas of the brain.
speech is held in a queue until each step has been completed.
years of practice have widened the central bottleneck.
items.evidence: Highly practised, automatic activities, such as walking or chewing, can proceed alongside others with little interference
items.note: D distorts 'highly practised' and contradicts Okafor's view that the bottleneck cannot be widened; B is never mentioned.

items.stem: What point does the writer make about the time lost each time a person switches task?
options: It is too brief to be measured reliably in a laboratory.
It varies according to how complex the two tasks are.
It is small in itself but becomes significant when added up.
It disappears if people are told to forget the previous task.
items.evidence: Such figures sound trivial, yet they accumulate over a working day.
items.note: A contradicts the text (laboratories do measure it); D reverses Marsh's finding that the earlier task lingers even when participants are told to forget it.

items.stem: What does the writer say about the 2009 study of heavy media users?
options: Its findings have been confirmed by all subsequent research.
It proved that multitasking damages the ability to concentrate.
It compared university students with professionals working in the media.
It did not establish which factor was the cause and which the effect.
items.evidence: which is a reminder that the direction of cause is far from settled
items.note: B is the tempting misreading: the study showed an association, and the writer stresses that the causal direction is unknown.

items.stem: The writer suggests that the attention paid to 'supertaskers' is misleading because
options: people who consider themselves good at multitasking frequently perform poorly.
they are less rare than the original research suggested.
their abilities have only been tested in driving simulators.
they performed well only on the memory problems.
items.evidence: the people most confident of their ability to multitask are often among those who do it worst
items.note: C mentions the simulators, which are in the text, but the writer does not criticise the research method; D contradicts 'no measurable decline in either task'.

items.text: A basic limitation of the mind can be reduced through training.
items.evidence: contending that the central bottleneck is not fixed but can be narrowed with sufficient practice
items.note: Okafor (E) takes the opposite view: the bottleneck is a bridge that no effort can widen.

items.text: A tendency to multitask may result from an existing difficulty in concentrating.
items.evidence: favours the second explanation, arguing that the habit is more a symptom than a cause

items.text: Improvements gained from practice tend to be restricted to the activity that was practised.
items.evidence: participants became much better at the game itself but showed no improvement on unrelated measures of attention

items.text: Attention is still partly taken up by a task after it has been abandoned.
items.evidence: participants who were interrupted mid-task performed less well on the next one

items.text: Organisations often value the appearance of activity more than genuine results.
items.evidence: many firms end up rewarding staff for looking busy rather than for what they actually achieve

items.statement: The word 'multitasking' was first applied to machines rather than to people.
items.evidence: the term itself is borrowed, rather tellingly, from computing

items.statement: People who often use several media at once become more skilled at switching between tasks.
items.evidence: The evidence points, uncomfortably, the other way.
items.note: The writer says one might expect practice to help, but the evidence points the other way: heavy multitaskers were slower at switching.

items.statement: Supertaskers are more likely to be found among younger adults.
items.note: The text gives the proportion of supertaskers (two or three per cent) but says nothing about their age.

items.statement: Combining two activities is unproblematic when one of them needs little conscious attention.
items.evidence: is harmless precisely because one of the two tasks makes few demands on conscious thought
